scenes.name: Virginia: Teddy Riley, los Neptunes, Timbaland y Missy Elliott
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Teddy Riley, arquitecto del new jack swing (hip hop con pop y R&B), se mudó de Nueva York a Virginia Beach y buscó talento en los concursos de los institutos: Pharrell Williams (entonces Magnum the Verb Lord) y Chad Hugo, los Neptunes, coescribieron «Rump Shaker» de Wreckx-n-Effect y luego «Superthug» de Noreaga. Pharrell estuvo en S.B.I. con DJ Timmy Tim (Timbaland) y Magoo; Timbaland conoció a Missy Elliott y acabaron en Da Bassment Crew de DeVanté Swing (Jodeci), encerrados en un sótano sin radio ni tele: por eso inventaron su propio género. Timbaland triunfó con «Pony» de Ginuwine (1996), el One in a Million de Aaliyah y «Up Jumps da Boogie»; Missy, que prefería escribir para otros, sacó Supa Dupa Fly (1997) y allanó el camino de Nicki Minaj, Lizzo o Megan Thee Stallion. En los 2000 parecía que todos los éxitos de la radio los producía alguien de Virginia: sintetizadores, voces moduladas, samples internacionales para Clipse, Jay-Z, Britney Spears o Justin Timberlake.

podcast.title: Production of Gwen Stefani's "Hollaback Girl" (2005)
podcast.body: The hip hop production duo The Neptunes, consisting of Pharrell Williams and Chad Hugo, co-wrote and produced Gwen Stefani's massive hit "Hollaback Girl." Their work contributed to the song's "hybridization of hip hop beef with pop rock sass," demonstrating their ability to bridge genres for mainstream success. "it was co-written and produced by the Neptune's, the hip hop production duo of Ferel Williams and Chad Hugo."

podcast.title: Production of "Hot in Here"
podcast.body: Production wizards Pharrell Williams and Chad Hugo, known as The Neptunes, were responsible for producing Nelly's 2002 Song of the Summer, "Hot in Here." They achieved this by taking an old Chuck Brown go-go record, amplifying its heat "high enough to make you quote take off all your clothes," and integrating St. Louis rapper Nelly's "Dirty South Style." "In 2002, production wizards The Neptune's, Ferel Williams and Chad Hugo, took an old Chuck Brown gogo record, turned up the heat high enough to make you quote take off all your clothes and added St. Louis rapper Nellie who spelled the word here with two Rs, Dirty South Style."
